case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Constitution and federal venue statutes permit prosecuting a defendant under 18 U.S.C. § 1519 in a district where the defendant performed no falsification conduct, based solely on the location of the federal investigation the defendant allegedly intended to obstruct.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 1519 (falsification of records in federal investigations); U.S. Const. art. III, § 2, cl. 3 and Sixth Amendment Vicinage/Venue Clauses (trial where the crime was committed); 18 U.S.C. § 3237(a) (continuing offense venue principles, as a background framework).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Venue must be tied to where the crime was 'committed,' which in this Court’s venue doctrine focuses on the statute’s essential conduct elements (the actus reus), not merely the statute’s intent element or contemplated downstream effects. For § 1519, the essential conduct is 'falsifies/makes a false entry in a record/document' (and related verbs) done knowingly; Abouammo’s alleged falsification conduct occurred in Seattle, not the Northern District of California. Allowing venue wherever an investigation happens to be located (or where effects are 'contemplated') would untether venue from where the defendant acted, create an amorphous and government-chosen forum, and expand venue based on facts not charged in the indictment or found by the jury. Petitioner also argues the government’s fallback claim at oral argument—that a separate metadata record was created in San Francisco—is forfeited and, in any event, lacks record support that Abouammo knowingly created a falsified record in that district.
case_analysis.respondent_position: A § 1519 prosecution may be brought in the district of the federal investigation that the defendant intended to obstruct because the obstructive act is directed at and targets that proceeding/investigation, making the investigation district a proper locus of the offense. In the government’s view, § 1519 is an obstruction statute whose gravamen includes the defendant’s intent to impede a specific federal matter; therefore venue may lie where that matter is pending or conducted, even if the physical falsification occurred elsewhere. The government also points to broader principles used in inchoate/obstruction contexts (and analogies to conspiracy venue concepts) to argue the offense is not limited to the defendant’s physical location. As an additional argument raised late, the government suggested that a document copy/metadata record may have been created in San Francisco, which could independently supply venue if credited.
key_precedents: United States v. Cabrales, 524 U.S. 1 (1998)
Whitfield v. United States, 543 U.S. 209 (2005)
Hyde v. United States, 225 U.S. 347 (1912)
United States v. Socony-Vacuum Oil Co., 310 U.S. 150 (1940)
United States v. Trenton Potteries Co., 273 U.S. 392 (1927)
Pinkerton v. United States, 328 U.S. 640 (1946)
Carpenter v. United States, 484 U.S. 19 (1987)
Ciminelli v. United States, 598 U.S. 306 (2023) (discussed in provided materials as background re property/fraud theory)
United States v. Kellington, 217 F.3d 1084 (9th Cir. 2000) (cited in the appendix materials)
United States v. Alston, 974 F.2d 1206 (9th Cir. 1992) (cited via Kellington quote in the appendix materials)

John Roberts.reasoning: The respondent’s best argument—that § 1519 is a continuing obstruction offense whose locus follows the federal investigation or “matter”—still improperly converts the statute’s object-of-intent circumstance into an essential conduct element, in tension with Cabrales and our locus-delicti cases. Justice Kagan’s point is decisive for me: because § 1519 covers falsification done “in contemplation of” a matter even before any investigation exists, the investigation’s situs cannot be what constitutionally anchors venue without an express congressional choice. Justice Barrett’s comparison to § 1512(i) reinforces the minimalist, text-based inference: when Congress wants proceeding- or investigation-based venue, it says so, and we should not imply it here. A narrow holding—venue lies where the falsification conduct occurred (or where part of it occurred under ordinary § 3237(a) principles), not solely where downstream investigative activity happens—protects Article III and the Sixth Amendment while avoiding unnecessary pronouncements about other tampering scenarios.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondent’s best argument—that § 1519 is a “continuing” obstruction offense whose venue tracks the location of the federal matter or investigation—fails under the statute’s text: the essential conduct is the falsification/destruction/concealment, while the “intent to impede” and “in relation to or contemplation of” clauses describe mens rea and circumstance, not geographically locating conduct. Chief Justice Roberts’s point about Congress’s explicit venue rule in § 1512(i) is decisive for a textualist: we may not infer an investigation-situs venue provision into § 1519 without diluting Article III and the Sixth Amendment. Cabrales remains controlling by analogy because venue cannot rest on downstream investigative activity in another district when the charged acts occurred elsewhere, and Rodriguez-Moreno does not help the government absent multiple essential conduct elements in different places. As Justice Barrett notes, the government’s late “metadata copy” theory cannot salvage venue on this record because it was not the indicted and jury-found knowing falsification conduct in the forum district.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s best contention—that § 1519 is a continuing obstruction offense whose venue follows the affected federal “matter” or investigation—still impermissibly converts an object-of-intent circumstance into a geographic conduct element. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, our locus-delicti framework looks to the statute’s essential conduct, and here the only conduct is the knowing falsification/destruction/concealment itself; the “in relation to or contemplation of” language underscores that an investigation’s situs cannot be an element because the statute reaches pre-investigation conduct. Justice Thomas’s comparison to § 1512(i) is particularly persuasive: Congress knows how to authorize investigation-based venue explicitly, and the absence of such a clause in § 1519 counsels against reading one in, consistent with Cabrales’s rejection of downstream-effects venue. The government’s fallback “metadata copy” notion, even if theoretically relevant in another case, cannot sustain venue on this record because it was not the charged and jury-found basis for a knowing falsification act in the Northern District of California.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The government’s strongest theory—that § 1519 is a continuing obstruction offense and venue can follow the affected federal “matter” or investigation—still collapses venue into an intent/effects framework that Cabrales rejects when the defendant’s charged conduct occurred elsewhere and Congress did not specify venue. As Justice Kagan underscores, § 1519 reaches acts done merely “in contemplation of” a matter even before any investigation exists, making the investigation’s situs an especially unstable and government-controllable hook that would invite forum selection and burden defendants of limited means. I also agree with Chief Justice Roberts that the statute’s essential conduct is the knowing falsification/making of a false entry, and on this record that conduct is in Seattle; the government’s late metadata-copy fallback cannot substitute for an indicted, tried, and jury-found act of knowing falsification in the Northern District of California. Rodriguez-Moreno does not alter that conclusion because § 1519 lacks multiple essential conduct elements spanning districts; it has conduct plus mens rea, and mens rea cannot constitutionally do the venue work.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—that § 1519 is an obstruction statute whose venue should follow the federal investigation’s situs—still treats an object-of-intent/circumstance as if it were an essential conduct element, which Cabrales squarely rejects absent an explicit venue rule. Chief Justice Roberts’s comparison to § 1512(i) is especially persuasive on the textual point: Congress knows how to authorize proceeding- or investigation-based venue and did not do so in § 1519, so we should not infer it. Rodriguez-Moreno does not move the ball for the government because § 1519’s only essential conduct is the falsification/destruction itself; the “intent to impede” clause is mens rea and cannot relocate the locus delicti. I also agree with Justice Barrett that the government’s metadata-copy fallback cannot sustain venue on this record because it was not the charged and jury-found knowing falsification conduct in the Northern District of California, and endorsing it would invite forum selection inconsistent with the venue guarantees.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The government’s best argument remains that § 1519 is an obstruction statute whose venue should track the affected federal matter or investigation, but as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan stress, that recharacterizes an object-of-intent circumstance as an essential conduct element, contrary to Cabrales and our locus-delicti framework. Rodriguez-Moreno supports the government only when the statute itself contains multiple essential conduct elements spanning districts; here the actus reus is the falsification/destruction/concealment, while the “intent to impede” and “in relation to or contemplation of” clauses supply mens rea and scope, not geography. Justice Barrett’s point about Congress’s express venue rule in § 1512(i) but silence in § 1519 is especially persuasive under a textualist approach: we should not imply an investigation-situs venue provision that Congress omitted. The “metadata in San Francisco” fallback cannot salvage venue on this record absent an indicted and jury-found knowing falsification act in that district.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The government’s best point is that § 1519 is an obstruction statute and, under continuing-offense principles, venue should track the situs of the affected federal “matter” or investigation; but as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, our locus delicti cases (Cabrales; Rodriguez-Moreno) require tying venue to essential conduct elements, and § 1519’s conduct is the falsification/concealment/making false entry—not the downstream investigation location. Kagan’s observation that § 1519 applies even “in contemplation of” a matter (when no investigation yet exists) is especially damaging to any investigation-situs venue rule because it makes venue depend on a non-element circumstance and invites forum selection. Justice Thomas’s point about Congress’s explicit venue choice in § 1512(i) reinforces, for an institutionalist approach, that we should not imply an investigation-location rule Congress did not enact. On this record, the late metadata-copy theory cannot salvage venue absent a charged and jury-found knowing falsification act in the Northern District of California, so venue lies where the falsification conduct occurred (Seattle), subject only to ordinary § 3237(a) “part of the offense” principles.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The government’s strongest point remains that § 1519’s “in relation to or contemplation of” language could make the federal matter an operative circumstance and thus permit venue where that matter is investigated, but—consistent with Justice Kagan’s observation—that clause expands temporal reach (including pre-investigation conduct) rather than adding an essential conduct element that can constitutionalize venue in a distant forum. Chief Justice Roberts’s comparison to § 1512(i) is particularly persuasive under a textualist methodology: when Congress wants venue keyed to an investigation or proceeding, it says so, and we should not infer such a rule in § 1519. Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno still point to the locus delicti as the falsification/destruction itself; treating mens rea or contemplated effects as a venue anchor would erode Article III and the Sixth Amendment’s vicinage protections. Finally, even if a “metadata copy” theory might matter in another case, Justice Thomas is right that it cannot sustain venue here absent a charged, tried, and jury-found knowing falsification act in the Northern District of California.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The government’s strongest position—that § 1519’s purpose of protecting federal investigations justifies venue where the investigation sits—still treats an intent/circumstance as if it were an “essential conduct element,” which Cabrales warns against, and it risks turning venue into a government-selected forum untethered from the defendant’s own acts. Chief Justice Roberts’s point is most persuasive to me on the constitutional stakes: Article III and the Sixth Amendment are not satisfied by locating venue based on downstream investigative activity rather than where the falsification was committed. Justice Kagan’s comparison to § 1512(i) reinforces the statutory inference: Congress knows how to authorize proceeding- or investigation-based venue expressly and did not do so in § 1519, especially given that § 1519 reaches acts done “in contemplation of” a matter when no investigation yet exists. The late “metadata copy” theory cannot salvage venue on this record because, as Justice Sotomayor notes, it was not charged and tried as a knowing falsification act in the Northern District of California, and adopting it would dilute procedural fairness protections the venue clauses are meant to secure.

John Roberts.reasoning: The Constitution’s venue guarantees (Art. III, §2, cl. 3; Sixth Amendment) require tying venue to where the crime was “committed,” and our cases instruct that locus delicti generally turns on the statute’s essential conduct elements. Under 18 U.S.C. § 1519, the essential conduct is the knowing falsification/making of a false entry (or destruction/concealment) of a record; the government’s theory would rest venue primarily on the intended target investigation’s location—an effects/intent-based approach that Cabrales rejected when Congress has not specified venue. Nothing in § 1519, unlike provisions such as 18 U.S.C. § 1512(i), supplies an investigation-location venue rule, and reliance on a late-raised “metadata copy” theory is not a sound basis to sustain venue where the indictment and jury findings did not establish knowing falsification conduct in the charging district. A narrow ruling holding that § 1519 venue lies where the falsification conduct occurred (or where some part of that conduct occurred under ordinary continuing-offense principles) best respects precedent and avoids an amorphous, government-selected forum.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Article III, § 2 and the Sixth Amendment require trial in the State and district “where the crime shall have been committed,” which must be determined from the statute’s text and the location of its essential conduct elements. Under § 1519, the core actus reus is “falsif[ying]” or “mak[ing] a false entry” in a record or document; the “with the intent to impede, obstruct, or influence” clause is mens rea and cannot relocate venue to the district where an investigation happens to sit. Cabrales holds venue may not rest on intent or downstream effects when the charged conduct occurred elsewhere, and nothing in § 1519 (unlike § 1512(i)) authorizes investigation-based venue; any reliance on a late-raised “metadata” theory does not alter that the indictment and proof must tie venue to where the knowing falsification was committed.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Article III and the Sixth Amendment require trial "where the crime shall have been committed," and our venue cases generally locate that place by identifying the statute’s essential conduct and asking where that conduct occurred. Under 18 U.S.C. § 1519, the proscribed conduct is the knowing falsification, destruction, or concealment of records; the government’s proposed venue rule would rest venue primarily on the location of a federal investigation that the defendant merely intended to obstruct—an intent/effects theory that untethers venue from where the defendant acted. United States v. Cabrales instructs that, absent a clear congressional venue specification, venue does not follow downstream consequences when all criminal acts occurred elsewhere; Congress knew how to authorize investigation-based venue (e.g., § 1512(i)) but did not do so in § 1519. The late-raised metadata-copy theory cannot salvage venue on this record because it was not the government’s charged, tried, and proved locus of the § 1519 falsification conduct.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Article III and the Sixth Amendment require trial “where the crime was committed,” and our venue cases look to the statute’s essential conduct elements—the actus reus—rather than a defendant’s intent or the downstream location of a federal matter. Under 18 U.S.C. § 1519, the prohibited conduct is falsifying or making false entries in records; on this record, that conduct occurred in Seattle, and allowing venue to hinge solely on the location of the investigation would untether venue from where the defendant acted and risk government forum selection. United States v. Cabrales instructs that venue cannot be based on related proceedings or effects in another district when the charged conduct itself occurred elsewhere, and nothing in § 1519 or § 3237(a) clearly makes this an investigation-location offense. The government’s late metadata theory cannot cure that problem where it was not charged and lacks record support that petitioner knowingly falsified a record in the Northern District of California.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Article III and the Sixth Amendment require trial “where the crime was committed,” and our venue cases look to the statute’s “essential conduct elements,” not a mens rea element or contemplated effects. Under § 1519, the only conduct element is the knowing act of falsifying/making a false entry (or destroying/covering up) a record; the “intent to impede” clause describes purpose but does not relocate where the act was committed, especially because § 1519 reaches conduct done “in relation to or contemplation of” a matter even when no investigation is pending. Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno therefore point to venue where the falsification occurred (here, Seattle), not where an investigation happened to be located, and the government’s late metadata theory cannot supply venue absent a charged, jury-found, knowing falsification in that district. This rule is textually grounded, workable, and avoids the government-chosen forum problems that follow from tying venue to investigative situs alone.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Article III and the Sixth Amendment require trial “where the Crime shall have been committed,” and our cases fix that location by identifying the statute’s essential conduct elements, not its mens rea or anticipated effects. Under § 1519, the actus reus is to “falsif[y],” “cover[] up,” or “make[] a false entry” in a record or document; as in Cabrales, venue cannot be bootstrapped to a different district based solely on where some related investigation sits when the charged falsification conduct occurred elsewhere. Section 1519 does not require any obstruction to occur (only an “intent to” impede), so the investigation’s location is not an element—much less an essential conduct element—capable of anchoring venue, and any “metadata in San Francisco” theory appears both forfeited and unproven as knowing falsification in that district. Where Congress wants venue to follow an affected proceeding, it knows how to say so (cf. 18 U.S.C. § 1512(i)), and we should not expand venue by implication in a way that dilutes the Constitution’s vicinage protection.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1519 contains no venue clause, so under Article III and the Sixth Amendment we determine venue from “the nature of the crime alleged and the location of the act or acts constituting it,” focusing on the statute’s essential conduct (actus reus) elements. See United States v. Cabrales, 524 U.S. 1 (1998); Rodriguez-Moreno, 526 U.S. 275 (1999). The essential conduct in § 1519 is “falsif[ying],” “mak[ing] a false entry,” or similar record-tampering acts, and here the alleged falsification conduct occurred in Seattle, not the Northern District of California; locating venue solely where an investigation happens to be based would improperly rest venue on an intent/circumstance element and invite government forum selection untethered to where the crime was committed. The government’s conspiracy analogies (Hyde/Whitfield) do not fit because § 1519 is not a continuing agreement offense, and its late metadata theory cannot expand venue absent record support that petitioner knowingly falsified a record in that district.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Article III and the Sixth Amendment require trial “where the crime was committed,” and this Court’s venue cases ask where the statute’s essential conduct elements occurred, not where the Government later feels investigative effects. Under 18 U.S.C. § 1519, the relevant conduct is the knowing act of “falsif[ying],” “conceal[ing],” or “mak[ing] a false entry” in a record; the investigation-related language chiefly supplies the object of the defendant’s intent, which does not by itself establish venue in the investigation’s district. Cabrales holds venue cannot rest on downstream connections to another district when the charged conduct took place elsewhere, and nothing in § 1519 (unlike statutes with explicit venue provisions, cf. 18 U.S.C. § 1512(i)) authorizes venue based solely on the investigation’s location. The Government’s late metadata theory cannot expand venue absent a charged, jury-found, and record-supported showing that petitioner knowingly falsified a record in the Northern District of California.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Article III and the Sixth Amendment require trial “where the crime was committed,” and when Congress has not specified venue for § 1519, our locus-delicti inquiry looks to the statute’s essential conduct elements—i.e., where the defendant “falsifies” or “makes a false entry”—not merely where an intended investigative effect is felt. Under Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno, venue cannot be anchored solely to downstream consequences or a related proceeding’s location when the charged conduct occurred elsewhere; here, the alleged falsification conduct occurred in Seattle, not the Northern District of California. Treating the investigation’s situs as sufficient would create a government-chosen, amorphous forum untethered to the defendant’s acts, undermining procedural fairness and the Vicinage/Venue guarantees. The government’s late metadata theory does not cure that defect absent a properly preserved, record-supported showing that the defendant knowingly falsified a record in that district, consistent with § 1519’s mens rea.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether venue for an 18 U.S.C. § 1519 prosecution can be laid in the district where the targeted federal investigation is located even if all of the defendant’s falsification conduct occurred elsewhere, based on the offense’s intent-to-obstruct element and contemplated effects.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. art. III, § 2, cl. 3; U.S. Const. amend. VI (Vicinage and venue requirements); Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 18; 18 U.S.C. § 1519 (falsification of records in federal investigations) (and the broader statutory venue framework for “continuing offenses,” 18 U.S.C. § 3237(a), as background).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues venue is improper in a district where no “essential conduct element” (i.e., the actus reus—making, altering, destroying, or falsifying a record/document) occurred, and that the Ninth Circuit’s rule—allowing venue wherever an investigation was located or where obstructive effects were contemplated—unconstitutionally expands venue by relying on intent and potential effects rather than conduct. Petitioner also contends the government’s fallback claim (that a copy/metadata version of the record was created on servers in the prosecuting district) was forfeited and, in any event, lacks evidentiary support because there was no proof the defendant knowingly created a record in that district or that any relevant server/location facts tie the actus reus there. Petitioner emphasizes this is not an immunity argument—only a constraint on the permissible place of trial—and warns the government’s approach would make venue unpredictable, manipulable, and detached from statutory text and jury-found facts.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent argues venue is proper in the district of the federal investigation at which the obstructive conduct was directed, on the theory that § 1519 is inherently aimed at obstructing an investigation/matter and thus the offense is ‘committed’ where the investigation is carried out (or where the obstructive objective is centered). The government characterizes § 1519 as sufficiently inchoate/obstruction-focused that the locus of the proceeding/investigation supplies a legitimate venue hook even if the physical falsification occurred elsewhere, and it analogizes to obstruction-related venue doctrines and to conspiracy-style concepts of offenses extending beyond the defendant’s immediate location. The government also suggests that, as a factual matter, the creation or existence of an additional document/copy (e.g., metadata) in the prosecuting district could supply conduct occurring there (though petitioner disputes forfeiture and proof).

United States v. Rodriguez-Moreno, 526 U.S. 275 (1999)
Whitfield v. United States, 543 U.S. 209 (2005)

United States v. Socony-Vacuum Oil Co., 310 U.S. 150 (1940)
Carpenter v. United States, 484 U.S. 19 (1987)

United States v. Percoco, 598 U.S. 319 (2023) (noted in the excerpt’s background chain)
Pinkerton v. United States, 328 U.S. 640 (1946) (referenced in oral argument discussion of conspiracy liability)

United States v. Alston, 974 F.2d 1206 (9th Cir. 1992) (quoted in joint appendix excerpt)

John Roberts.reasoning: I remain with Petitioner because the Government’s best argument—treating § 1519 as “investigation-directed” so venue lies where the investigation sits—cannot be squared with Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno, which require us to anchor venue to the statute’s essential conduct elements, not anticipated effects or the locus of a contemplated federal matter. Justice Barrett’s point is decisive on text: the “intent to impede” language is mens rea (at most a circumstance), and reading it to relocate venue would effectively create an effects-based venue rule Congress chose to provide expressly elsewhere (as Justice Kagan notes with § 1512(i)) but omitted here. Even if a “server/metadata” theory could matter in a different record, Justice Alito is right that venue must rest on charged-and-proven conduct in the district under Rule 18 and the Venue/Vicinage Clauses, not a post hoc account of where digital traces landed. Minimalism and institutional legitimacy counsel a narrow holding: for § 1519, absent an express venue provision or proved conduct in the forum, venue lies where the falsification/alteration/destruction occurred.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Government’s best argument—that §1519 is “obstruction-like” and thus venue should track the situs of the affected investigation—cannot overcome the Constitution’s venue commands (Art. III; Sixth Amendment) as applied through our locus-delicti cases. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch stress, Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno require identifying the statute’s essential conduct elements, and §1519 criminalizes the act of falsifying/altering/destroying records; the “intent to impede” language is mens rea (as Justice Barrett notes) and cannot itself supply venue. The contrast with Congress’s explicit venue expansion in §1512(i), emphasized by Justice Kavanaugh, is powerful textual evidence that we should not infer an effects-based venue rule here. The server/metadata fallback does not change the analysis on this record because, as Justice Alito explains, venue must rest on charged and jury-found facts showing knowing falsification conduct in the prosecuting district, not post hoc investigative consequences elsewhere.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Respondent’s strongest point is that § 1519 is inherently “investigation-directed,” so venue should track the situs of the federal matter; but as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas stress, Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno require us to anchor venue in the statute’s essential conduct elements, and here that conduct is the knowing falsification/alteration/destruction of a record, not the later location of an investigation the defendant hoped to affect. Treating the intent-to-obstruct clause as a venue hook would improperly convert mens rea (or, at most, a circumstance) into conduct, inviting the very forum shopping the Venue and Vicinage Clauses were designed to prevent—especially telling given Congress included an explicit venue expansion in § 1512(i) but omitted one in § 1519, as Justice Barrett emphasizes. The Government’s metadata/server fallback cannot carry venue on this record because, consistent with Rule 18 and the jury-trial guarantee, it was not the charged-and-proven basis showing that the defendant knowingly falsified anything in the prosecuting district. Nothing in colleagues’ discussion identifies a precedent that would justify an effects-based venue rule here without Congress’s clear instruction, so I remain with Petitioner.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument—that § 1519 is “obstruction-like” so venue should lie where the federal investigation sits—still collapses into an intent/effects theory that Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno reject when the statute’s essential conduct is the knowing falsification/alteration/destruction itself. Chief Justice Roberts’s emphasis on the Venue and Vicinage Clauses’ anti–forum-shopping function is not abstract formalism; it highlights how an investigation-situs rule would be unpredictable and disproportionately burdensome for defendants with fewer resources to litigate far from home, undermining access to justice. Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett reinforce the key textual point: Congress included an express venue expansion in § 1512(i) but not in § 1519, so we should not add by implication what Congress omitted. And as Justice Alito notes, the government’s server/metadata fallback cannot salvage this case because venue must rest on charged and jury-found facts tying the defendant’s knowing falsification conduct to the prosecuting district, consistent with Rule 18 and the constitutional guarantees.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest pitch—that § 1519 is “obstruction-like” so venue should follow the situs of the federal matter or investigation—still tries to do indirectly what Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno forbid: use effects/objective location to supply venue when the statute’s essential conduct is the act of falsifying/altering/destroying records. Chief Justice Roberts’s point that Congress expressly expanded venue in § 1512(i) but not here is powerful textual context; as a pragmatic textualist, I’m reluctant to invent an investigation-district hook that would predictably invite forum shopping and post hoc selection of a convenient district. Justice Alito’s caution about the government’s server/metadata fallback also matters: even if a technological pathway could sometimes show conduct in-district, venue must rest on charged-and-proven knowing falsification conduct there, not a generalized theory that records “touch” a server. On administrability and statutory coherence, anchoring venue to where the falsification occurred is the clearest rule and best fits the Constitution’s venue guarantees.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—that § 1519 is obstruction-like and thus venue should track the location of the obstructed federal matter—still collapses under our locus-delicti framework because it makes venue turn on intended effects rather than any conduct element Congress prescribed. As Chief Justice Roberts (and Justice Barrett) emphasize, Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno require us to identify the statute’s essential conduct; here that is the knowing falsification/alteration/destruction of records, while the intent-to-impede clause is mens rea (or at most a circumstance) and cannot relocate venue by itself. Congress’s decision to include an express venue expansion in § 1512(i) but omit one in § 1519, highlighted by Justice Kagan and Justice Thomas, is strong textual evidence against importing an investigation-situs rule by implication. The government’s server/metadata fallback might matter in a different case, but as Justice Alito notes it would require charged-and-proven knowing falsification conduct in the charging district, not merely that investigative consequences or copies landed there.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The respondent’s best point is that §1519’s “in relation to or contemplation of” a federal matter conceptually ties the offense to the investigation’s situs, but under Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno venue still turns on the statute’s essential conduct elements—here, the knowing falsification/alteration/destruction—not the hoped-for effects or the government’s later choice of investigative forum. Chief Justice Roberts’s administrability and forum-shopping concerns are decisive for me institutionally: an effects/intent-based venue rule would be unpredictable, manipulable, and would effectively supply a venue provision Congress conspicuously included elsewhere (as Justice Barrett notes with §1512(i)) but omitted in §1519. Justice Alito’s point about the server/metadata fallback reinforces that we cannot uphold a broad investigation-district theory absent charged-and-proven facts showing knowing falsification conduct occurred in the prosecuting district. On text, precedent, and practical legitimacy grounds, I remain with Petitioner that venue lies where the falsification conduct occurred unless Congress clearly provides otherwise.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—that § 1519 is an obstruction statute whose venue should follow the situs of the obstructed federal matter—still depends on effects and purpose rather than the statute’s essential conduct, which our locus-delicti cases require us to identify. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno direct venue to where the proscribed acts occurred; here the text criminalizes “falsif[ying]” or “mak[ing] a false entry” (conduct) done with an obstructive intent (mens rea), not the existence or location of an investigation. Justice Thomas’s observation about Congress’s express venue rule in § 1512(i) is especially probative textually: Congress knew how to tie venue to a proceeding’s district and chose not to do so in § 1519, so we should not infer that expansion. The government’s server/metadata fallback remains case-specific and cannot justify venue absent charged and jury-found facts establishing that knowing falsification conduct occurred in the prosecuting district, consistent with Rule 18 and the Venue/Vicinage Clauses.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The respondent’s best argument—that § 1519 is “obstruction-like” so venue should lie where the federal matter or investigation is located—does not overcome Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno’s essential-conduct framework; it asks us to let mens rea/anticipated effects do work the statute’s conduct elements do not. Chief Justice Roberts’s manipulability point is especially persuasive to me as a matter of procedural fairness: tying venue to an investigation’s situs would allow post hoc forum selection, undermining the Article III and Sixth Amendment venue/vicinage constraints and Rule 18’s fairness baseline. Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett further reinforce that Congress’s inclusion of an express venue provision in § 1512(i) but not § 1519 is strong contextual evidence against judicially creating an effects-based venue rule. The government’s server/metadata fallback cannot salvage venue on this record because, as Justice Sotomayor notes, it was not clearly charged and jury-found as knowing falsification conduct in the prosecuting district.

John Roberts.reasoning: Article III and the Sixth Amendment require trial “where the crime shall have been committed,” and our venue cases ask first what conduct the statute criminalizes and then where that conduct occurred. Under Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno, venue generally lies where the statute’s “essential conduct elements” took place; for § 1519 that is the knowing falsification/alteration/destruction of records, not the later location of a federal investigation or the defendant’s contemplated obstructive effects. Allowing venue based on the situs of the targeted investigation would expand venue on intent/effects alone, creating the unpredictability and prosecutorial forum-shopping the Venue and Vicinage Clauses were designed to prevent, and Congress has not supplied an express venue provision for § 1519 comparable to § 1512(i). The government’s alternative “metadata/server” theory is, at best, case-specific and cannot justify a broad rule untethered to jury-found conduct in the charging district under Rule 18.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Article III and the Sixth Amendment require trial in the State and district “wherein the Crime shall have been committed,” which turns on the locus delicti—the location of the acts constituting the offense, not merely the intended obstructive objective or downstream effects. Section 1519’s text criminalizes the knowing act of “falsif[ying]” or “mak[ing] a false entry in” a record with a specified intent; under Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno, venue lies where the essential conduct element (the falsification) occurred, and intent alone cannot relocate the crime to the district housing the investigation. Allowing venue wherever the investigation is located would detach venue from the defendant’s conduct and expand prosecutorial forum choice beyond what the Constitution’s venue clauses and Rule 18 permit; if Congress wished to authorize proceeding-based venue, it knew how to do so expressly (cf. 18 U.S.C. § 1512(i)). The government’s metadata/server theory, in any event, cannot cure a constitutional venue defect absent jury-found facts tying knowing falsification conduct to the chosen district.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Article III and the Sixth Amendment require trial “where the crime shall have been committed,” and § 1519 contains no special venue clause authorizing prosecution wherever an investigation happens to be located. Under Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno, venue turns on the statute’s “essential conduct elements,” here the knowing act of falsifying/altering/destroying a record, not the defendant’s obstructive intent or the contemplated effects on an investigation in another district. Treating the situs of the investigation as a venue hook would untether venue from the defendant’s conduct, invite forum shopping, and effectively rewrite § 1519 to include an obstruction-of-a-proceeding location element Congress did not adopt (contrast 18 U.S.C. § 1512(i)). The government’s late “metadata/server” theory cannot salvage venue on this record where it was not charged or found by the jury and does not establish knowing falsification conduct in the prosecuting district.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Constitution’s venue and vicinage guarantees (Art. III, § 2, cl. 3; Amend. VI), implemented through Rule 18, require trial where the offense was “committed,” which this Court in Cabrales instructs we determine by identifying the offense’s essential conduct elements and locating where that conduct occurred. Under § 1519, the essential conduct is “mak[ing], alter[ing], destroy[ing], mutilat[ing], conceal[ing], cover[ing] up, falsif[ying], or mak[ing] a false entry” in a record; the statute’s intent-to-obstruct language does not convert the situs of a contemplated investigation into a venue-creating act, and Rodriguez-Moreno’s acknowledgement of multiple venues still turns on where conduct elements occur, not merely effects or objectives. Allowing venue wherever the investigation is located would be unpredictable and susceptible to prosecutorial manipulation, imposing unfair burdens on defendants—including those with fewer resources—without clear congressional authorization (and Congress’s decision to include an explicit venue provision in § 1512(i) underscores that it knew how to do so when intended). The government’s late “metadata/server copy” theory cannot salvage venue absent indictment and jury-found facts tying knowing falsification conduct to the prosecuting district.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1519 contains no venue provision, so under Art. III, § 2, the Sixth Amendment, and Rule 18, venue turns on where the offense was “committed,” i.e., where the essential conduct elements occurred. Under Rodriguez-Moreno, we identify the statute’s essential conduct elements (here, “mak[ing], alter[ing], destroy[ing], mutilat[ing], conceal[ing], cover[ing] up, falsif[ying], or mak[ing] a false entry” in a record) and do not treat the intent-to-obstruct component as a venue-creating “conduct” element; Cabrales likewise rejects venue based on downstream effects or the locus of related proceedings when the charged conduct happened elsewhere. Allowing venue wherever the investigation sits would effectively convert § 1519 into an effects-based venue statute without clear congressional direction (contrast Congress’s explicit venue choices in other obstruction provisions like § 1512(i)), raising predictability and manipulability concerns inconsistent with constitutional venue constraints. The government’s late-breaking metadata/server theory cannot salvage venue on this record where it was not the tried-and-found basis for where the falsification conduct occurred.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Article III and the Sixth Amendment require trial in the State and district where the crime was “committed,” and where Congress (as in § 1519) has supplied no venue clause we identify the statute’s essential conduct elements and locate where that conduct occurred. Under § 1519, the proscribed conduct is “mak[ing], alter[ing], destroy[ing], mutilat[ing], conceal[ing], cover[ing] up, falsif[ying], or mak[ing] a false entry” in a record; the intent “to impede, obstruct, or influence” a federal matter is a mens rea/circumstance element that does not itself create venue where an investigation happens to sit. Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno teach that venue may not rest on downstream effects or forum connections divorced from where the defendant’s own statutorily proscribed acts took place; allowing venue wherever the investigation is located would untether venue from the text and invite manipulation. The government’s server/metadata fallback, even if not forfeited, cannot supply venue absent proof of a knowing falsification act in the charged district consistent with § 1519’s conduct requirement.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Constitution’s venue and vicinage commands (Art. III, § 2, cl. 3; Amend. VI), implemented by Rule 18, require trial where the offense was “committed,” which this Court determines by identifying the statute’s conduct elements and locating where that conduct occurred. Under Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno’s locus-delicti framework, § 1519’s essential conduct is the knowing falsification/alteration/destruction of records, and the statute’s intent-to-obstruct element—standing alone—does not relocate venue to the district of the contemplated investigation. Allowing venue wherever an investigation is located or where effects are contemplated would make venue unpredictable and manipulable, and Rodriguez-Moreno expressly reserved (rather than adopted) any effects-based venue theory. Because Congress did not include an express venue provision in § 1519 (unlike 18 U.S.C. § 1512(i)), the Court should not expand venue beyond the districts where the defendant’s falsification conduct occurred.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Article III and the Sixth Amendment require trial “in the State and district wherein the crime shall have been committed,” and where a statute like § 1519 contains no venue clause, we locate the offense by identifying its “essential conduct elements” and where those acts occurred. Under Rodriguez-Moreno, intent and other “circumstance elements” do not themselves supply venue; here, the only essential conduct is “knowingly…falsif[ying]…any record [or] document,” and all such conduct occurred outside the investigation district. Cabrales reinforces that venue may not be laid solely where downstream effects are felt or where related proceedings are located when the charged conduct took place elsewhere. Because § 1519 does not criminalize obstruction effects as an actus reus and Congress has elsewhere supplied explicit obstruction venue rules (e.g., § 1512(i)), the Government’s investigation-district theory would impermissibly expand venue beyond what the text and this Court’s precedents permit.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Article III and the Sixth Amendment require trial “where the offense was committed,” and when § 1519 contains no venue clause, we locate venue by identifying the statute’s “essential conduct elements” and where that conduct occurred. Under Rodriguez-Moreno and Cabrales, the essential conduct here is the knowing falsification/alteration/destruction of a record; the intent-to-obstruct component is a mens rea (or at most a circumstance element) that cannot, standing alone, relocate venue to the district of the investigation without diluting constitutional and Rule 18 constraints. Allowing venue based on the investigation’s location or contemplated effects would make venue manipulable and unpredictable, especially where (as here) the government’s server/metadata theory was not clearly charged or jury-found, raising procedural-fairness concerns. Congress knows how to provide obstruction-specific venue rules (cf. § 1512(i)); absent that clarity, we should not expand § 1519 venue beyond districts where the charged falsification conduct occurred.
